splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected before the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions can be selected after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans to use more current data in their calculations.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to extend the period of supervision and find violations after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that courts lack authority to apply a judicially-created fugitive tolling doctrine to supervised release absent explicit statutory authorization, as doing so extends punishment beyond the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than the separate requirements in § 2255(h) alone.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar applies to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, categorically barring them from raising any claim previously presented in a successive collateral attack.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome affects whether election administration rules can be challenged before an election or must wait until post-election disputes arise.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election laws pre-election based on competitive injury from rules that may affect vote counting.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules absent a more concrete showing of injury.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous provisions that carry criminal consequences.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions. The Third Circuit held deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold lenity takes priority. This split has deepened after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity, as a centuries-old canon, takes precedence over deference to agency or Commission interpretations in criminal and sentencing contexts.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold that defendants are disqualified only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that any one criterion disqualifies. This split produces dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) is unambiguously conjunctive, meaning a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria are met.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) operates disjunctively, meaning possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1's expansion of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses is a valid, deferential interpretation of the guideline or an impermissible expansion beyond the text. This split affects career-offender sentencing enhancements for many defendants.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline under Stinson v. United States and survives Kisor scrutiny, such that conspiracy qualifies as a controlled substance offense.

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds the guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally controlled, or whether any state-controlled substance qualifies. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-only controlled substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is federally controlled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's amendments to mandatory minimums, can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in law can serve as the basis for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit holds they cannot contribute at all, while other circuits allow them as a factor. This affects thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences under pre-First Step Act mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot contribute
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may contribute
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the totality of circumstances in determining whether extraordinary and compelling reasons exist for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 60-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter criminal appeal deadline applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for challenges that go beyond the fact or duration of confinement but implicate terms such as BOP transfer decisions under the First Step Act. The Eighth Circuit acknowledged this unresolved conflict that has persisted for over half a century.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that affect the duration of imprisonment must be brought through habeas corpus, not civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights claims are available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights claims (e.g., Bivens or § 1983) to challenge conditions of confinement even where habeas might also be available.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether § 348(f)(1)(A) of the Bankruptcy Code means that appreciation in property value between the original Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held it belongs to the estate, creating a split with other circuits.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor who converts in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for violations of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the need to sanction the breach of trust and protect public safety.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts expressly to punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that revocation sentences must focus on the breach of the court's trust and public safety, not retributive punishment for the underlying violation.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is impermissible
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must be based on the breach of the court's trust and public safety considerations, not retributive punishment for the underlying violation of conditions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' under Mohawk Industries. Other circuits have taken different approaches to the collateral order doctrine's application in sealing contexts, creating potential tension.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that medical privacy is a value of high order warranting immediate appellate review, and denial of a motion to seal medical records satisfies the collateral order doctrine's requirements.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated on appeal from final judgment.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Kravetz (discussing privacy interests)

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on the standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, including issues of liability and available remedies. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, indicating a potential circuit split on the applicable legal framework for fair treatment in hospitality, retail, and service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that business operators face broader liability for discrimination claims, with more expansive remedies available to aggrieved customers.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards apply to discrimination claims against business operators, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
